Brussels on foot

Wizzy knows 50 places in Brussels, from the big sights to the corners most people walk straight past. Start a walk, put your phone away, and Wizzy taps you on the shoulder when there's something worth looking up at.

The must-sees

  • Atomium

    Landmark · 1958

    It was built for the 1958 World’s Fair, designed by the engineer André Waterkeyn. It was meant to stand for six months and has become the symbol of the city.

  • Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula

    Church

    It was built over about three centuries, from the 13th to the early 16th. Belgian royal weddings and funerals are held here.

    Look for: Inside, the carved oak pulpit shows Adam and Eve being driven out of Paradise.

  • Grand-Place

    Square

    French artillery destroyed most of the square in 1695, and the guilds rebuilt their houses within a few years. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.

    Look for: At the top of the Town Hall tower, a gilded St Michael stands over the slain devil.

  • Horta Museum

    Museum · 1901

    Horta built the house between 1898 and 1901. It is one of four of his Brussels buildings on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

    Look for: Follow the staircase up: its iron curves climb towards a glass roof that pulls daylight down through the middle of the house.

  • Manneken Pis

    Landmark · 1619

    Jérôme Duquesnoy the Elder made the statue in 1619; the one on the corner is a copy. The boy owns more than a thousand costumes, many of them gifts from abroad.

  • Palace of Justice

    Civic building · 1883

    Joseph Poelaert designed it but died in 1879, four years before it was finished. Next to it a free lift links the upper town with the Marolles below.

  • Parc du Cinquantenaire

    Park

    It was laid out for the 50th anniversary of Belgian independence in 1880; the arch was finished in 1905. The wings house museums of art and history, cars and military history.

    Look for: On top of the arch, the bronze chariot is driven by a figure of Brabant raising the national flag.

  • Royal Palace

    Palace

    The king works here but lives at the castle of Laeken in the north of the city. The palace usually opens its doors to visitors in summer.

    Look for: Check the flagpole on the roof. The flag flies when the king is in the country.

  • Royal Saint-Hubert Galleries

    Shopping · 1847

    Designed by Jean-Pierre Cluysenaar and opened in 1847, it was one of the first covered shopping arcades in Europe. Its three sections are the King’s, the Queen’s and the Princes’ galleries.

    Look for: Above the central entrance, find the Latin motto Omnibus omnia, ‘everything for everyone’.

How it works

  1. Open Wizzy in Brussels and tap Start walk, or pick a ready-made walk.
  2. Put your phone in your pocket. Wizzy runs in the background, even with the screen locked.
  3. When you pass a place, you get a ping. Open it for the story, or keep walking.

Every place you see gets stamped in your Brussels passport. Your location stays on your phone. No ads, no tracking.
